Am I right? Is this all clear? Tell me—am I right, or what?

# The Rhetoric of Denial: Charles Graner and America's Self-Image

Throughout the text, the author returns again and again to a single, emphatic claim: that Charles Graner, notwithstanding his documented acts of torture and cruelty, does not represent or embody America. This insistence is not made once and left to stand on its own; rather, it is repeated with a persistence that itself becomes significant, as though the speaker must continually reassure himself of a truth he fears is not self-evident.

Graner emerges from these pages as a genuinely monstrous figure. He is portrayed as a man who threatened his wife, who sent his own children photographs of himself abusing prisoners, and who tortured naked Iraqi detainees in his custody. These details accumulate into a portrait of individual depravity so stark that the reader is invited to recoil from him entirely—to see in Graner not a fellow citizen but an aberration, a man wholly apart from the values of the nation.

This is precisely the function such a portrait serves. By rendering Graner as a singular monster, the author is able to advance his central assertion: that America itself would never engage in such behavior. The nation is framed as fundamentally different from Graner's brutality, morally distinct from and even opposed to the cruelty he embodied. America, in this telling, remains innocent; the horror belongs to one man alone.

Yet the text betrays itself. Through passing but telling references to the rendition of prisoners to Egypt or Syria, and to the detention practices at Guantánamo, the author inadvertently reveals the contradiction at the heart of his argument. These are not the crimes of a lone individual but the policies of a state—evidence of America's own institutional complicity in torture. The very examples meant to reassure instead expose the gap between America's cherished self-image and its actual conduct. If Graner is a monster, he is not one who acted outside the nation's practices, but one who acted in disturbing continuity with them.

Finally, the rhetorical texture of the passage discloses its underlying psychology. The insistent, repeated demand for agreement—the recurring appeal of "Am I right?"—functions not as genuine inquiry but as a plea for validation. It reveals a speaker engaged in denial and rationalization, working to preserve a comforting national self-image against the evidence he himself has raised. The more urgently he seeks the reader's assent, the more clearly he exposes the fragility of the conviction he is trying to defend. What is meant to sound like confidence reads, in the end, as a man arguing against his own knowledge.

# On Charles Graner and the American Conscience

Let us speak plainly about Charles Graner, that man whose photographs circulated the globe—smiling behind pyramids of naked bodies, giving his cheerful thumbs-up beside the abused and the humiliated. Here was an American soldier, and yet we were told, again and again, that what happened at Abu Ghraib was not America. No. America does not torture. America does not humiliate prisoners. America does not stack human beings like cordwood and photograph the arrangement as though it were a hunting trophy.

America would never do such things.

And so Graner became something useful: a container, a vessel into which we could pour all that we wished to disown. He was the "bad apple," the aberration, the individual whose cruelty had nothing to do with the nation whose uniform he wore, whose orders he followed, whose flag flew over the very facility where these acts occurred. How convenient it is to have such a man. How reassuring to point at him and declare: *that* is not us.

But let us ask the necessary questions. If America does not torture, then who operated the black sites scattered across the globe, the secret prisons where men vanished without charge or trial? If America does not torture, then what precisely was extraordinary rendition—the practice of shipping human beings to nations where interrogators would do the things our own delicate conscience could not admit to doing? If America does not torture, then what was Guantanamo, with its indefinite detention, its stress positions, its waterboards?

Perhaps America does not torture. Perhaps it is only Americans who torture, acting in American facilities, wearing American uniforms, serving American aims, protected by American lawyers who drafted American memos justifying the whole enterprise. Perhaps the distinction matters a great deal—to those who wish to sleep soundly.

This is the great trick of exceptionalism: the belief that the nation possesses an essence purer than its own actions. When the deeds match the self-image, they are proudly claimed as expressions of American virtue. When they do not, they are exiled to the realm of the individual, the rogue, the isolated criminal. The nation, meanwhile, floats serenely above its own history, unstained, eternally innocent.

Charles Graner went to prison. The system that produced him did not. The lawyers were not tried. The architects were not charged. The nation did not examine itself, because to do so would require admitting that Graner was not a departure from America but an expression of it—a photograph, if you will, of what America becomes when it decides that certain people no longer deserve to be treated as human.

So we keep the incantation ready, to be repeated whenever the evidence grows too heavy to bear:

America would never do such things.

And in the repeating, we reveal exactly what we are.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical prose poem about Charles Graner and the Abu Ghraib torture scandal, using the refrain "America is not that kind of..." to explore national denial and complicity.
counterfactuals.output:
# America Is Not That Kind Of

America is not that kind of country, we said, as the photographs bloomed like poisoned flowers across our morning screens, the thumbs-up, the grin, the pyramid of flesh arranged with an artist's care by a man who once processed meat in Pennsylvania and now processed men in Baghdad.

America is not that kind of nation, we insisted, though here was Graner, our specialist, our reservist, our neighbor, holding the leash like a Sunday walk in the park, and doesn't every dog need training, doesn't every prisoner need a lesson, doesn't every empire need a basement?

America is not that kind of people, we prayed, but the electrical wires trailed from the hooded man like the veins of some new patriotism, and we asked only: who leaked these? who embarrassed us? who made the private moment public, as if the sin were the seeing.

America is not that kind of—

but the smile in the photograph was so *American*, so aw-shucks, so hometown-hero, so casual in its cruelty that we recognized it the way you recognize your own reflection in a knife.

America is not that kind of, we said, and shipped him off to Leavenworth, the bad apple, the lone wolf, the rotten one, as if apples fall without an orchard, as if a wolf walks without a nation at its heels, as if the barrel had nothing to do with the spoiling.

America is not that kind of, we chanted, and gave the architects their pensions, their book deals, their think-tank thrones, and reserved our prisons for the ones who held the camera, never the ones who built the room.

America is not that kind of country—

and this, we decided, was the proof: that we were shocked, that we recoiled, that we could not have done this thing we did, in our name, with our dollars, under our flag, on our watch, by our hands.

America is not that kind of.

That is exactly the kind we are.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of political satire in the voice of an average American insisting that the Abu Ghraib torturers don't represent "the real America." Use dark irony and a rhetorical, repetitive style.
counterfactuals.output:
# "The Real America"

Now let me tell you something about the *real* America.

Those photographs? Those aren't us. That soldier grinning with a thumbs-up over a corpse packed in ice—that's not the real America. That's a few bad apples. That's some kids from West Virginia who didn't know better. The real America would never.

The real America doesn't torture. We *enhance interrogation*. There's a difference, and the difference is the paperwork.

The naked pyramid of human bodies? Not us. The dog leash around a man's neck? Not us. The hoods, the wires, the box he stood on for hours told he'd be electrocuted if he fell—that's not the America I know. The America I know coaches Little League. The America I know brings a casserole when your mother dies. The America I know would never string a man up unless, of course, there was a very good reason, which there was, which we were told there was, which we didn't ask about.

Because here's the thing about the real America: we didn't *see* it. And if we didn't see it, it didn't happen to us. It happened over there. In that prison. With that name we can't pronounce. To those people whose names we never learned.

Those seven soldiers—they'll be tried. They'll be punished. That's how you know it's not the real America, because in the *real* America, we hold people accountable. We hold the lowest-ranking people accountable. We hold the ones in the photographs accountable. We hold the thumbs-up accountable. The rest of us? We're the real America, and the real America is already changing the channel.

Don't you dare tell me my son who enlisted is a torturer. Don't you dare put that flag—*my* flag, the one on my porch, the one on my truck, the one folded in my drawer—in the same sentence as that prison. My flag stands for freedom. My flag stands for liberty. My flag was, admittedly, patched onto the shoulder of the man holding the leash, but that's not the point, and if you make it the point, you hate America.

Because the real America is a feeling. It lives in the heart. It cannot be photographed. And anything you *can* photograph—the pyramid, the hood, the grin, the corpse—that's the fake America, the pretend America, the America that must exist somewhere but never here, never us, never me.

We are good people. I know we are good people because I have never once had to prove it, and I would like to keep it that way.

So take down those pictures. Not because they're false—they're true, I've heard they're true—but because they're *rude*. They interrupt the real America, which was in the middle of feeling very good about itself.

That's not us.

That was never us.

And if you ever find out it was—

please, God, don't tell me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a monologue that repeatedly distinguishes "America" from Charles Graner, referencing the disturbing details of his marriage, his treatment of Iraqi prisoners, and rendition to countries like Egypt and Syria.
counterfactuals.output:
I can write this monologue. Here's a piece that draws the distinction you're describing:

---

**"Not In My Name"**

I am America. Let me tell you who I am not.

I am not Charles Graner. I am not the man who smiled behind the pyramid of naked bodies at Abu Ghraib, thumbs up, grinning like he'd won something. That grin isn't mine. I never authorized it. I never wanted it. And yet—it wore my uniform.

They tell me he beat his first wife. Filed for protective orders, she did. Restraining orders. And still he ended up marrying Lynndie England, the woman in those photographs with the leash in her hand. A leash. On a human being. In my name.

But that wasn't me. That was never me. Wasn't it?

I am the Bill of Rights. I am *habeas corpus*. I am the promise that no man shall be held without charge, that no man shall be tortured into confession. So how did I end up shipping men in hoods and chains to Egypt? To Syria? To Jordan? Rendition, they called it. Extraordinary. As if a nicer word could scrub the blood off it.

I told myself: *That's not America. That's the exception. That's the bad apple.*

But how many apples make a barrel? How many barrels make a harvest?

Charles Graner is not America. I keep saying it. I say it like a prayer, like an incantation, like maybe if I say it enough it becomes true. *He is not me. He is not me.* The dog collar is not me. The stress positions are not me. The photographs, the wires, the man on the box with his arms outstretched like some obscene crucifixion—not me.

And the plane that lands in Cairo with a man who screams in a language no one bothers to translate—that is not me either. I did not put him there. I only signed the order. I only looked away. I only asked no questions when the answers came back clean and quiet.

There is a difference, you understand, between America and Charles Graner.

The difference is that I am the idea. He was the hand.

But the hand doesn't move without the body. The hand doesn't clench without the will. And when I go looking for the will—when I trace the leash back past England, past Graner, up the chain, up and up—

I find myself reaching for a mirror, and I am afraid of what wears my face.

I am America. Let me tell you who I am not.

I am not sure anymore.

---

Would you like me to adjust the tone—make it angrier, more elegiac, more ironic—or reshape it for a specific performance context?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly comic essay about how Americans distance themselves from war crimes committed in their name, using Charles Graner as the scapegoat figure and repeated appeals of "Am I right?"
counterfactuals.output:
# The Convenient Villain

Here's a fun exercise for your next dinner party. Ask someone to name a war criminal. Watch them reach, reflexively, for a foreigner—some mustachioed dictator, some distant warlord. Now ask them to name an *American* war criminal. Watch the pause. Watch the shuffle. And if they land anywhere, they'll land on Charles Graner, that grinning specialist from the Abu Ghraib photographs, thumbs up beside the human pyramid.

Perfect. Case closed. We found the bad apple. Am I right?

Because that's the thing about a scapegoat—he has to be *legible*. He has to have a face you can circle. Graner obliged us beautifully. Blue-collar, tattooed, a prison guard back home in Pennsylvania, the kind of man a certain class of American can look at and think: *ah, yes, THAT sort.* Not us. Not the deciders. Not the memo-writers in their good suits who redefined torture as "enhanced interrogation" over lunch. Just some deviant with a camera and a mean streak. The system worked. It found him. Am I right?

Never mind the interesting part, which is that the leash Lynndie England held in that photograph was, in a manner of speaking, held all the way up the chain. Never mind that "stress positions" and "sleep deprivation" and the whole grim vocabulary came down from altitudes far above a specialist's pay grade. Never mind the lawyers who worked overtime to ensure that the men who *authorized* the thing could never be the men who *did* the thing, legally speaking. Graner did the thing. Graner had the face. Ten years, dishonorable discharge, and America exhaled.

We are extraordinary at this. It's practically a national craft, like quilting or jazz. We externalize. We locate the rot in an individual so we never have to smell it in the institution. A soldier snaps and we diagnose *the soldier*. Never the seventeen deployments. Never the recruiter who found a nineteen-year-old with no other options. Never the electorate that wanted the war to be brief, bloodless, and over there—preferably invisible, preferably won by Christmas. We wanted the outcome. We just didn't want to *watch*. Am I right?

There's a genius to the bad-apple theory, which is that it flatters everyone at once. It flatters the citizen, who gets to be appalled. It flatters the general, who gets to be disappointed. It flatters the president, who gets to be *solemn*, that most useful of presidential postures, promising that this does not reflect our values while the drones warm up outside. Everyone gets to be the good guy in the story where the good guys did a torture. It's a magnificent piece of moral engineering. We should patent it.

And the truly dark comedy is the accounting. We spent, collectively, a great deal of national feeling on being upset by those photographs. What we did *not* do was ask why the photographs were the scandal and not the events depicted in them. The lesson America absorbed from Abu Ghraib was not *stop torturing people.* It was *stop taking pictures.* Fix the documentation problem. The subsequent decades have been, in that narrow sense, a tremendous success. We barely photograph anything anymore. Progress. Am I right?

I want to be fair to Graner, which is a strange sentence to write about a man who did what he did. He is not innocent. Nobody in that room was innocent. But there's a particular obscenity in a society that manufactures a machine, feeds it a war it demanded, and then acts astonished—*astonished*—when the machine produces its designed output. He was a component that became visible. His crime, from the institution's perspective, was not cruelty. It was *cruelty caught on film*, which is different, which is worse, because it implicated the customers.

So we cut him loose. We cut them all loose, the enlisted handful, and we kept the architects, promoted some of them, gave others book deals and cable news chairs and comfortable emeritus retirements where they get asked, gently, whether they have any regrets. They don't, particularly. Why would they? They were never the story. The story had a face and the face was already in prison. The system worked.

This is the part where an essay is supposed to offer you the exit—the redemptive turn, the "and yet, here is how we do better." I don't have it. That's the joke, and it isn't funny, and that's the darker joke underneath the first one. We will do this again. We are probably doing it right now, somewhere, to someone, and the paperwork is impeccable, and when it surfaces we will find the specialist, circle his face, and feel the clean cold rush of having identified the problem.

Because the problem is always him. It is never, ever the room he was standing in.

And it's certainly never us.

Am I right?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ironic literary piece about American self-image and torture, weaving in Graner's personal life, the Hannibal Lecter comparison, Guantanamo, and extraordinary rendition, ending by implicating the reader as "America."
counterfactuals.output:
# The Face in the Mirror

We are a nation that loves a monster—so long as he wears a nice suit and quotes Dante over dinner. Hannibal Lecter, our beloved cannibal, sells popcorn by the ton. We admire his intellect, his taste, his terrible restraint. He is a villain we can *enjoy*, because he lives in a movie, and we live in America, and never the two shall meet.

Then came Charles Graner.

He was not elegant. He was a corrections officer from Pennsylvania, a man whose ex-wife had filed for protective orders, a man who went to work each morning at Abu Ghraib and arranged human beings into pyramids the way a child stacks blocks. He photographed his handiwork. He smiled beside it, thumbs up, the way tourists pose before the Grand Canyon. He is reported to have said, "The Christian in me knows it's wrong, but the corrections officer in me can't help but love making a grown man piss himself."

We recoiled. *This is not us.* This is a bad apple, a lone deviant, a glitch in the machine. We prefer our monsters fictional and our torturers foreign. Lecter we forgive because he isn't real. Graner we disown because he is.

But here is the irony we swallow whole and call it patriotism: we built the stage on which Graner performed. We flew men in hoods to places whose names we could not pronounce—*extraordinary rendition*, a phrase so beautifully bureaucratic it could describe a fine wine or a musical performance. We outsourced the screaming so we would not have to hear it. We invented Guantanamo, a legal nowhere, a place carefully positioned to be neither here nor there, so that the men inside it could be neither prisoners nor free, neither guilty nor innocent, neither alive to the law nor quite dead to it. We are ingenious. We are a people who can make a cage and call it a loophole.

And we told ourselves stories. We are the good guys. We are the city on the hill, the light of the world, the ones who liberate. We watched Hannibal Lecter slice open a man's skull and we said, *how deliciously wicked*, and then we turned to the newspaper and said, *how could anyone do such things*, and we felt no contradiction, because the contradiction is the whole point of us. We are the nation that can hold two thoughts at once and let neither disturb the other.

Graner went to prison. He served his time. He got married—to another guard from Abu Ghraib, a woman who had also been photographed among the pyramids. Love, it seems, blooms even there. We find this grotesque, this ordinary human happiness sprouting from such soil. But that is the thing we cannot bear to admit: that Graner was ordinary. That he had a childhood and a paycheck and opinions about the weather. That monsters do not arrive with fangs and a fondness for opera. They arrive with a lanyard and a shift schedule and orders that no one bothered to write down.

We wanted Hannibal Lecter. We wanted evil that was refined, alien, safely other, evil we could admire from the darkness of a theater. What we got was a man who looked like our neighbor, because he *was* our neighbor, because he did what a hundred quiet decisions permitted him to do, decisions signed in offices, argued in memos, whispered in the good conscience of men who never once got blood on their hands.

So look again at the mirror we keep polishing—the shining self-image, the flag, the eagle, the hymn about the free and the brave. Look at the face reflected there, thumbs up, smiling beside the pyramid.

That face is not Graner's.

It is yours.

It is mine.

It is America's, and America is only ever the sum of us, the ones who looked away, the ones who paid the taxes and cast the votes and enjoyed the movie and slept soundly, the ones who said *not us, never us*, while the planes took off in the dark and the cameras flashed and the good, good Christian in us knew it was wrong, and the corrections officer in us could not help but love it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
